item.title: Proxmox VE 9 high availability: HA rules, fencing and a failover you have actually tested
item.description: Proxmox VE HA restarts a dead node's guests elsewhere, but only on a cluster that is ready for it. How the CRM, LRM and watchdog fence a node, the new node and resource affinity rules that replaced HA groups in Proxmox VE 9, the shutdown policy, maintenance mode, and a pulled-power test.
item.content:encoded:
High availability is the feature most people build a Proxmox VE cluster for: a node dies at 3 a.m. and its important guests are running again on another node before anyone wakes up. Proxmox VE does this with two daemons, a watchdog and a set of rules. This post explains how those pieces fit together, adds guests to HA, writes placement rules (which changed in Proxmox VE 9), walks through a node failure step by step, and covers planned shutdowns and maintenance.

The trap

HA gets switched on for a cluster that is not ready for it: two nodes and no QDevice, or guests whose disks live on local storage with no replica. When a node fails, nothing restarts, or the surviving node fences itself.

The second trap is using HA as a substitute for backups. HA restarts the guest. It does not undo whatever was wrong with it.

The documented requirements are short: at least three cluster nodes (or two plus a QDevice) for reliable quorum, shared storage for the guests (or replicated storage, with a data-loss window back to the last replica), hardware redundancy, and a watchdog.

The HA stack in two daemons

Every node runs:

  • pve-ha-lrm, the local resource manager. It starts and stops HA guests on its own node, following the state the CRM requests.
  • pve-ha-crm, the cluster resource manager. One node's CRM is the active master at any time. It tells the LRMs what to run, moves guests when something fails and handles fencing.

Both rely on locks in the cluster file system and on a watchdog. While a node is healthy and quorate, its daemons keep resetting the watchdog timer. If the node loses quorum or the HA daemons stop working, the timer runs out and the watchdog resets the node.

Why fencing matters

Before a guest from a failed node can start somewhere else, the cluster must be certain the failed node is not still running it, perhaps cut off from the network but still writing to shared storage. Starting a second copy would corrupt the disk. Making sure the node is really off is called fencing.

Proxmox VE fences with watchdog timers. A node outside the quorate part of the cluster cannot reset its watchdog, so the watchdog resets it. Once the CRM master can take the failed node's lock, it knows the node has fenced itself and can recover its guests.

Without a configured hardware watchdog, Proxmox VE uses the Linux kernel's softdog, which the docs describe as reliable but not independent of the server's hardware. Hardware watchdog modules are blocked by default; to use one, name its module and reboot:

# /etc/default/pve-ha-manager
WATCHDOG_MODULE=iTCO_wdt

One warning from the docs worth repeating: never kill pve-ha-crm, pve-ha-lrm or watchdog-mux by hand. They manage the watchdog, and killing them can cause an immediate reset of the node.

Adding guests to HA

An HA resource is a type and an ID: vm:100, ct:110.

ha-manager add vm:100
ha-manager add ct:110 --state started --max_restart 1 --max_relocate 1
ha-manager config
ha-manager status

In the web interface it is Datacenter → HA → Resources → Add, or More → Manage HA on a guest.

--state is the requested state: started, stopped, disabled or ignored. Once HA manages a guest, ordinary qm start and qm stop simply change its requested state. max_restart is how often HA retries starting it on the same node after a failed start, and max_relocate how often it tries another node; both default to 1.

ha-manager set vm:100 --state stopped     # stop and keep stopped
ha-manager migrate vm:100 pve2            # live migration
ha-manager relocate vm:100 pve2           # stop, move, start
ha-manager remove vm:100                  # stop managing (does not stop it)

Before you add a guest, check it can run on every node HA might pick: disks on shared or replicated storage, bridges with the same names on every node, and no passthrough devices. If a dependency exists on only some nodes, restrict the guest to them with a strict node affinity rule.

HA groups became HA rules in Proxmox VE 9

Earlier releases used HA groups to say which nodes a guest prefers. Proxmox VE 9.0 deprecated them in favour of HA rules, stored in /etc/pve/ha/rules.cfg. Existing groups are migrated to node affinity rules automatically once every node runs Proxmox VE 9; if anything looks wrong afterwards, the upgrade guide points to the active CRM's log, journalctl -eu pve-ha-crm.

Node affinity: which nodes a guest runs on

# Prefer pve1 for the firewall VM; any node is fine if pve1 is down
ha-manager rules add node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --resources vm:100 \
  --nodes pve1
# Make it a hard requirement instead
ha-manager rules set node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --strict 1
# Ordered preference: pve1 first, then pve2 or pve3 equally
ha-manager rules add node-affinity ha-core \
  --resources vm:101,ct:110 --nodes "pve1:2,pve2:1,pve3:1"
# Keep these guests off pve3 (the small node)
ha-manager rules add node-affinity not-pve3 --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:200,vm:300 --nodes pve3

Node affinity rules are not strict by default: if none of the listed nodes is available, the guest may run elsewhere. With --strict 1 it is restricted to the listed nodes and stopped if none of them is up. Priorities are relative; higher numbers win, and nodes without a number get 0. failback, a per-resource property that defaults to on, moves a guest back to its highest-priority node when that node returns.

Resource affinity: guests together or apart

# Two DNS servers should never share a node
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity dns-apart --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:120,ct:121
# An app and its database should stay together
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity app-with-db --affinity positive \
  --resources vm:130,vm:131

Resource affinity rules are the opposite: strict by default. A negative rule cannot list more resources than there are nodes.

Rules are checked for conflicts before they apply. A resource can be in only one node affinity rule, for example, and two resources cannot be kept both together and apart. A conflicting rule is disabled until you resolve it, so run ha-manager rules config after every edit.

What happens when a node dies

  1. Node pve2 loses power. Corosync on pve1 and pve3 stops hearing from it and forms a new membership without it. Two of three votes: still quorate.
  2. The CRM master marks pve2's HA guests as waiting for fencing (state fence).
  3. If pve2 were still running but cut off, it would be in a minority without quorum and unable to reset its watchdog, and the watchdog (60 seconds, per the docs) would reset it. A node with no power is already fenced in practice.
  4. Once the CRM can take pve2's lock, the node counts as fenced and its guests move to recovery.
  5. The CRM picks a node for each guest from the online, quorate nodes, narrowed by the affinity rules, and chooses the one with the lowest load. The guests start there.
  6. When pve2 comes back it rejoins the cluster, and guests with failback move back if a rule prefers it.

With Ceph or shared storage the guests start with every completed write intact. With ZFS replication they start from the last replica. And every guest that ran on the failed node now runs on fewer nodes, which the docs warn can overload small clusters: size each node so the others can carry its HA guests, or mark only what truly matters as HA.

Test it with the power cord

Before you trust HA with the firewall, test it with a disposable VM: add it to HA, then pull the power cord (not a clean shutdown) of the node running it. Watch ha-manager status on another node until the VM shows as started on its new home. A clean shutdown tests something else, the shutdown policy.

Planned shutdowns: pick a shutdown policy

A planned shutdown is not a failure, and HA handles it according to the cluster's shutdown policy, set in Datacenter → Options → HA Settings or in datacenter.cfg:

ha: shutdown_policy=migrate
  • conditional (the default): on shutdown, stop the guests and let other nodes take them over; on reboot, freeze them and start them again on the same node.
  • migrate: mark the node unavailable and live-migrate its HA guests away first; they return when it is back.
  • failover: stop the guests and recover them elsewhere if the node is not back soon.
  • freeze: stop and freeze the guests; nothing moves until the node returns.

The docs note that conditional is the default for backward compatibility and that some users find migrate behaves more as expected. One catch with migrate: a guest restricted by a strict node affinity rule to unavailable nodes makes the shutdown hang until you step in.

Maintenance mode for one node

For work on a single node, maintenance mode is the cleanest tool. It migrates the node's HA guests away and brings them back when you disable it:

ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance enable pve2
ha-manager status          # wait until no HA guests remain on pve2
# ... patch, reboot, replace hardware ...
ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance disable pve2

It can run from any node. The LRM shows maintenance as soon as the request is picked up, before every guest has moved, so watch the guest list rather than the status word. Maintenance mode survives a reboot and ends only when you disable it.

For work that could briefly break quorum everywhere, such as re-cabling the corosync network, Proxmox VE 9.2 added a cluster-wide switch: ha-manager crm-command disarm-ha freeze, then ha-manager crm-command arm-ha when you are done. While HA is disarmed it protects nothing, so keep the window short.

Checklist

  • Quorum survives one node down (three nodes, or two plus a QDevice).
  • Every HA guest's disks are on shared, Ceph or replicated storage.
  • Every rule in ha-manager rules config is enabled (no conflicts).
  • The shutdown policy is a deliberate choice, not the default by accident.
  • A pulled-power failover test of a disposable VM succeeded.
  • Each node can carry the HA guests of any one failed node.

item.title: Will this model fit on your GPU? Size a local LLM on paper before you pull it
item.description: When ollama ps shows a CPU/GPU split, your model did not fit and everything runs at the speed of system RAM. Parameters, quantization and the KV cache turn sizing into arithmetic: weights + context + overhead, worked through for Llama 3.1 8B, then checked against ollama ps.
item.content:encoded:
You download the biggest model your disk can hold, ask it a question, and wait. The answer arrives a word at a time, the CPU fans spin up, and ollama ps says 45%/55% CPU/GPU. The model did not fit in the card's memory, so part of it runs from system RAM, and the whole thing moves at the speed of that slow part. The opposite mistake is just as common: a tiny model that fits easily but cannot follow a two-step instruction.

Sizing is arithmetic, not guesswork. Three numbers decide whether a model fits: its parameters, its quantization, and the context you give it.

Parameters: what the "8b" means

A model's name usually carries its size: llama3.1:8b, qwen3:14b, gemma3:27b. The number is the parameter count in billions, the weights the model learned during training. More parameters generally means more knowledge and better reasoning, and always means more memory and slower answers on the same hardware.

At full 16-bit precision each parameter takes 2 bytes, so an 8-billion-parameter model is about 16 GB of weights. That is why the Ollama library lists llama3.1:8b-instruct-fp16 at 16 GB.

Mixture-of-experts models such as qwen3:30b or gpt-oss:20b hold all their parameters in memory but use only part of them for each word, so they can answer faster than a dense model of the same size. For sizing, what matters is the full size of the file you load.

Quantization: smaller numbers, smaller model

Quantization stores each weight with fewer bits. A model quantized to about 4 bits per weight is roughly a quarter the size of the 16-bit original, and in practice loses surprisingly little quality on most tasks. Ollama and llama.cpp use the GGUF file format, and the quantization is part of the tag:

  • Q8_0: about 8 bits per weight. Closest to the original, twice the size of Q4.
  • Q6_K, Q5_K_M: the middle ground.
  • Q4_K_M: about 4 to 5 bits per weight. The common default, and what Ollama gives you for a plain tag like llama3.1:8b.
  • Q3_K_M, Q2_K: smaller still, with a visible quality cost.
  • fp16 or bf16: no quantization at all.

Start at Q4_K_M. Move up only if you have memory to spare and can see a difference on your own prompts. Dropping to Q3 or Q2 to squeeze in a bigger model is usually worse than running a smaller model at Q4.

Context: the memory everyone forgets

The context window is how many tokens the model can see at once: the system prompt, the conversation so far, any retrieved documents and the answer it is writing. Ollama picks a default from the card's memory; its context-length page lists 4k tokens below 24 GiB of VRAM, 32k from 24 to 48 GiB and 256k at 48 GiB or more.

Context costs memory because the model keeps a KV cache: for every token in the window it stores a key and a value vector in every layer. The size per token comes straight from the model's architecture:

KV bytes per token = 2 (key and value) x layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per number

Llama 3.1 8B's published configuration has 32 layers, 8 key-value heads and a head size of 128. With a 16-bit cache:

2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes, about 0.13 MB per token
  4,096 tokens  ->  about 0.54 GB
  8,192 tokens  ->  about 1.07 GB
 32,768 tokens  ->  about 4.29 GB
131,072 tokens  ->  about 17.2 GB

That last line is the full context Llama 3.1 supports, and its cache alone is bigger than the 16-bit model. Long context is not free.

Two settings change the picture. Ollama can store the cache in 8-bit numbers: its FAQ lists f16 as the default, q8_0 as about half the memory with a very small loss in precision, and q4_0 as smaller still with a more noticeable loss. A quantized cache needs flash attention, which Ollama enables automatically where the hardware supports it. And parallel requests multiply context: with OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4, the FAQ says required memory scales with the number of parallel requests times the context length, so four parallel 8K conversations reserve as much cache as one 32K conversation.

The estimate

Add three things:

  1. Weights: the file size of the tag you pull.
  2. KV cache: per-token size times context length (times parallel requests).
  3. Overhead: compute buffers, the CUDA runtime and whatever else sits on the card. It varies by model, backend and driver; the examples below assume about 1 GB, and you confirm the real number on your own machine.

Llama 3.1 8B with an 8,192-token context, using the library's file sizes. These are estimates, rounded to a tenth of a gigabyte:

TagWeightsKV cache (8K, f16)Overhead (assumed)Estimate
8b-instruct-q4_K_M4.9 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 7.0 GB
8b-instruct-q5_K_M5.7 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 7.8 GB
8b-instruct-q8_08.5 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 10.6 GB
8b-instruct-fp1616 GB1.1 GB1.0 GBabout 18.1 GB

The same model at Q4_K_M as the context grows:

ContextKV cacheEstimate (f16 cache)Estimate (q8_0 cache)
4,0960.5 GBabout 6.4 GBabout 6.2 GB
8,1921.1 GBabout 7.0 GBabout 6.4 GB
32,7684.3 GBabout 10.2 GBabout 8.0 GB

Read the tables against your card. An 8 GB card runs the Q4_K_M model comfortably at the default context and gets tight at 8K. A 12 GB card has room for 8K at Q5_K_M, or 32K with a quantized cache. A 16 GB card can hold Q8_0 at 8K. Leave a margin: if the estimate is within a gigabyte of the card's total, expect Ollama to spill part of the model to system RAM.

Check it against reality

An estimate is a starting point. Load the model with the context you plan to use, then:

ollama ps

The SIZE column is what Ollama actually allocated, the CONTEXT column is the context it used, and the PROCESSOR column must say 100% GPU. If it shows a CPU/GPU split, pick a smaller quantization, a smaller context or a smaller model, and check again.

Picking the file

The Ollama library at ollama.com/library lists every model's sizes, context window and capabilities, and each tags page lists every quantization with its file size. ollama pull qwen3:8b downloads the default quantization; ollama pull llama3.1:8b-instruct-q5_K_M asks for a specific one.

Hugging Face hosts many more GGUF files, and Ollama can run them directly:

# Q4_K_M is used by default when the repository has it
ollama run hf.co/bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF

# Ask for a specific quantization by its tag
ollama run hf.co/bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF:Q8_0

Stick to repositories from the model's publisher or well-known quantizers, and read the model card, including the license, before you build anything on top. "Open" models come with very different licenses: as listed on Hugging Face in October 2026, Llama 3.1 uses the Llama 3.1 Community License and Gemma 3 the Gemma Terms of Use, while Qwen3, gpt-oss and Mistral 7B are Apache 2.0.

Checklist

  • You know your card's memory before you pick a model.
  • You start at Q4_K_M and move up only with memory to spare.
  • You estimate weights + KV cache + overhead before you pull.
  • You know the context you need, and that parallel requests multiply it.
  • ollama ps shows the SIZE you expected and 100% GPU after loading.
  • You have read the license of every model you build on.

item.title: Real HTTPS for your homelab Kubernetes apps without opening a port: k3s Traefik, cert-manager and a DNS-01 wildcard
item.description: Self-signed warnings on every app, or port 80 open to the internet for Let's Encrypt? Neither. A DNS-01 wildcard from cert-manager, served as Traefik's default certificate on k3s, gives every internal app a trusted certificate while nothing on your network is reachable from outside.
item.content:encoded:
Every web app in a homelab cluster should answer at a proper hostname with a certificate your browser trusts, and you should not have to forward a single port from the internet to get there. On k3s you already have most of the pieces: the Traefik ingress controller ships with it. Add cert-manager, one DNS-01 issuer and one wildcard certificate, and every app you route gets real HTTPS automatically.

The trap

There are two traps, one on each side.

The first is living with certificate warnings: self-signed certificates on every app, a browser you have trained to click "proceed anyway", and a password manager that refuses to autofill. That habit is exactly what an attacker on your network would rely on.

The second is fixing it the obvious way: opening port 80 to the internet so Let's Encrypt can run an HTTP-01 challenge. That publishes your lab to every scanner on the internet for the sake of a padlock icon.

The DNS-01 challenge avoids both. You prove you control the domain by creating a DNS record through your DNS provider's API. Nothing on your network has to be reachable from outside.

How a request reaches a pod

When something does not load, walk this path in order:

  1. Your browser asks LAN DNS for paperless.home.example.com and gets the private address of Traefik's LoadBalancer Service (for example 192.168.40.200, handed out by MetalLB).
  2. The node that holds that address receives the connection and hands it to a Traefik pod.
  3. Traefik terminates TLS, matches the hostname against its routes, and forwards the request to the app's ClusterIP Service.
  4. The Service sends it to one of the app's ready pods.

Step 1: check the Traefik that k3s installed

k3s installs Traefik from a bundled Helm chart into kube-system and registers an IngressClass called traefik. Because it is the only ingress controller in the cluster, it picks up standard Ingress objects without being told.

kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy,svc traefik
kubectl -n kube-system get helmchart traefik -o yaml | grep -i version

Change Traefik's settings with a HelmChartConfig named traefik, never by editing the generated chart manifest. One gotcha when you copy older snippets: the chart version k3s ships moved the Service type from service.type to service.spec.type, and the k3s documentation warns that the old key is silently ignored.

While you are there, redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS everywhere:

apiVersion: helm.cattle.io/v1
kind: HelmChartConfig
metadata:
  name: traefik
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  valuesContent: |-
    ports:
      web:
        http:
          redirections:
            entryPoint:
              to: websecure
              scheme: https
              permanent: true
kubectl apply -f traefik-config.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=traefik -w

k3s re-runs the chart with the merged values and Traefik restarts.

A note if you are following an older tutorial that installs ingress-nginx first: in November 2025 Kubernetes SIG Network and the Security Response Committee announced the retirement of ingress-nginx, with best-effort maintenance until March 2026 and no releases or security fixes after that. k3s already gives you Traefik. Translate those guides' Ingress objects to the traefik class, and review any nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/* annotations, because Traefik ignores them.

Step 2: install cert-manager

cert-manager watches Certificate objects, gets certificates from an issuer such as Let's Encrypt, stores them in Secrets and renews them before they expire. The project publishes its Helm chart in an OCI registry (v1.21.3 at the time of writing; check for the current release):

helm install cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \
  --version v1.21.3 \
  --namespace cert-manager --create-namespace \
  --set crds.enabled=true
kubectl -n cert-manager get pods

crds.enabled=true lets the chart install and upgrade cert-manager's CustomResourceDefinitions.

Step 3: a DNS-01 issuer

You need a domain you own, hosted at a DNS provider cert-manager can talk to. It supports several directly (Cloudflare, Route 53, Google Cloud DNS, Azure DNS, DigitalOcean and others) and many more through webhooks. With Cloudflare, follow cert-manager's documentation: create an API token, not the global API key, with Zone - DNS - Edit and Zone - Zone - Read, limited to your zone.

kubectl -n cert-manager create secret generic cloudflare-api-token \
  --from-literal=api-token='PASTE-THE-TOKEN'

Then a ClusterIssuer:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: you@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account
    solvers:
      - dns01:
          cloudflare:
            apiTokenSecretRef:
              name: cloudflare-api-token
              key: api-token

Create a second issuer named letsencrypt-staging with the server https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory. Staging has much more generous rate limits, so get everything working there first. The token secret lives in the cert-manager namespace because, for a ClusterIssuer, cert-manager looks for referenced secrets in its own namespace by default.

Step 4: one wildcard for every internal name

You could request one certificate per app. A single wildcard for *.home.example.com is simpler and has a privacy benefit: every certificate Let's Encrypt issues is published in public Certificate Transparency logs, and a wildcard publishes *.home.example.com instead of a list of every app you run. Wildcards can only be issued through DNS-01, which is one more reason to use it.

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: wildcard-home
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  secretName: wildcard-home-tls
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-staging        # switch to letsencrypt-prod when it works
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  dnsNames:
    - "home.example.com"
    - "*.home.example.com"
kubectl apply -f wildcard.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get certificate wildcard-home -w     # READY becomes True
kubectl describe certificaterequest -n kube-system          # if it does not

Once the staging certificate shows Ready, change issuerRef.name to letsencrypt-prod, apply again, and delete the old secret so cert-manager issues a fresh one.

Step 5: make it Traefik's default certificate

The certificate lives in kube-system, but an Ingress can only reference Secrets in its own namespace. Instead of copying the secret into every namespace, make it Traefik's default. Traefik serves the default certificate for any TLS connection that no more specific certificate matches:

apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: TLSStore
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  defaultCertificate:
    secretName: wildcard-home-tls

Now any Ingress under home.example.com that asks for TLS gets the wildcard automatically, with no secretName at all:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: whoami
  namespace: whoami
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: ["whoami.home.example.com"]
  rules:
    - host: whoami.home.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: whoami
                port:
                  number: 80

Plain Ingress is a fine choice here. The k3s documentation states that the traditional Ingress API is still supported and not planned for deprecation, and most Helm charts still generate it.

Keep internal names internal

DNS-01 means the certificate is public but the service is not. Nothing in public DNS points at your lab; the only public record cert-manager creates is a temporary TXT record during issuance. *.home.example.com resolves only through your LAN resolver's override to a private address, so from outside your network the names do not resolve and the address is unreachable.

For access from outside the house, use a VPN instead of a port forward. Once your phone is connected, it uses the LAN resolver and every app works exactly as it does at home.

Checklist

  • kubectl get ingressclass shows traefik, and Traefik settings live in one HelmChartConfig.
  • Plain HTTP redirects to HTTPS.
  • cert-manager is installed with crds.enabled=true.
  • The DNS provider credential is a scoped API token, stored in the cert-manager namespace.
  • Staging and production ClusterIssuers exist, and you proved the setup on staging first.
  • One wildcard Certificate is Ready and set as Traefik's default in a TLSStore.
  • No port is forwarded from the internet; remote access goes through a VPN.

item.title: Test your Compose ViewModels in milliseconds: fakes, runTest, the Main dispatcher and Turbine
item.description: The ViewModel holds a Compose screen's behavior and runs on the plain JVM, which makes it the best-value test in an Android app. A hand-written fake, a MainDispatcherRule, runTest's virtual time, Turbine for state sequences, and the StateFlow and stateIn traps that make these tests fail for the wrong reason.
item.content:encoded:
The ViewModel is where a Compose screen's behavior lives: what the screen shows while loading, what happens when the user saves, which error appears when the network fails. It is plain Kotlin and runs on the JVM, so its tests take milliseconds and need no emulator. That makes it the best-value test in an Android app. This post tests a small note editor's ViewModel with a fake repository, coroutine test dispatchers, Turbine and SavedStateHandle.

The code under test

The editor loads a note by id, lets the user change the title and body, and saves. Its state is a single StateFlow<EditorUiState>, and the important parts look like this:

class EditorViewModel(
    private val repository: NotesRepository,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,
) : ViewModel() {

    private val noteId: Long? = savedStateHandle.get<Long>("noteId")
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(EditorUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<EditorUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val note = noteId?.let { repository.getNote(it) }
            _state.update {
                it.copy(
                    title = savedStateHandle["draftTitle"] ?: note?.title.orEmpty(),
                    body = note?.body.orEmpty(),
                    isLoading = false,
                )
            }
        }
    }

    fun save() {
        val current = _state.value
        if (current.title.isBlank()) {
            _state.update { it.copy(error = "Title is required") }
            return
        }
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(isSaving = true) }
            when (val result = repository.save(noteId, current.title, current.body)) {
                is SaveResult.Ok -> _state.update { it.copy(isSaving = false, saved = true) }
                is SaveResult.Failed -> _state.update {
                    it.copy(isSaving = false, error = result.message)
                }
            }
        }
    }
    // onTitleChange() also writes savedStateHandle["draftTitle"]
}

NotesRepository is an interface. That one decision makes the ViewModel testable: a test can hand it anything that implements the interface.

Fakes, not mocks, by default

A mock (MockK, for example) is configured per test: you tell it what to return and afterwards verify which calls were made. A fake is a small, real implementation written by hand, usually backed by a map in memory. Google's testing guidance recommends fakes as the default test double, for practical reasons:

  • A fake behaves like the real thing, so tests check behavior ("after saving, the note is in the repository") rather than implementation details ("save was called once with these arguments").
  • A fake is written once and reused by every test. Mocks are configured again in every test.
  • Refactoring the ViewModel does not break tests that use a fake, as long as the behavior stays the same.

Keep mocks for the edges: a third-party class you cannot implement easily, or a check that something was not called.

class FakeNotesRepository : NotesRepository {
    private val notes = mutableMapOf<Long, Note>()
    private var nextId = 1L
    var failNextSave: String? = null
    var saveDelayMs = 0L

    fun seed(vararg seed: Note) {
        seed.forEach { notes[it.id] = it }
        nextId = (notes.keys.maxOrNull() ?: 0L) + 1
    }

    override suspend fun getNote(id: Long): Note? = notes[id]

    override suspend fun save(id: Long?, title: String, body: String): SaveResult {
        delay(saveDelayMs)                 // virtual time in tests
        failNextSave?.let { failNextSave = null; return SaveResult.Failed(it) }
        val note = Note(id ?: nextId++, title, body)
        notes[note.id] = note
        return SaveResult.Ok(note.id)
    }

    fun all(): List<Note> = notes.values.toList()
}

Step 1: replace the Main dispatcher

viewModelScope launches on Dispatchers.Main. On the JVM there is no Android main looper, so a test that creates this ViewModel fails with an error about the Main dispatcher missing. The fix is Dispatchers.setMain and Dispatchers.resetMain from kotlinx-coroutines-test, and the Android Developers coroutine testing guide recommends wrapping them in a JUnit rule so no test forgets:

class MainDispatcherRule(
    val testDispatcher: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher(),
) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) {
        Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
    }

    override fun finished(description: Description) {
        Dispatchers.resetMain()
    }
}

Every ViewModel test then starts with one line: @get:Rule val mainDispatcherRule = MainDispatcherRule().

Step 2: understand runTest and the two dispatchers

runTest runs the test body as a coroutine with virtual time: a delay(5_000) inside it completes instantly, while the test still sees five seconds pass. There are two test dispatchers, and the difference matters:

  • StandardTestDispatcher queues new coroutines. They do not run until the test yields, with advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), runCurrent() or by suspending. It is the default in runTest, and it lets you check intermediate states such as "saving is in progress".
  • UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts new coroutines eagerly until their first suspension. Simple tests read shorter, but you cannot observe the state between "launched" and "finished".

When MainDispatcherRule installs a test dispatcher as Main, runTest reuses its scheduler, so advanceUntilIdle() in the test also drives coroutines launched in viewModelScope.

Step 3: the first tests

class EditorViewModelTest {

    @get:Rule val mainDispatcherRule = MainDispatcherRule(StandardTestDispatcher())

    private val repository = FakeNotesRepository()

    private fun viewModel(noteId: Long? = null) = EditorViewModel(
        repository,
        SavedStateHandle(mapOf("noteId" to noteId)),
    )

    @Test fun saving_blank_note_shows_error_and_saves_nothing() = runTest {
        val vm = viewModel()
        advanceUntilIdle()

        vm.onTitleChange("   ")
        vm.save()
        advanceUntilIdle()

        assertThat(vm.state.value.error).isEqualTo("Title is required")
        assertThat(repository.all()).isEmpty()
    }

    @Test fun saving_shows_progress_then_marks_saved() = runTest {
        repository.saveDelayMs = 2_000
        val vm = viewModel()
        advanceUntilIdle()
        vm.onTitleChange("Groceries")

        vm.save()
        runCurrent()                       // the save starts, then suspends in delay()
        assertThat(vm.state.value.isSaving).isTrue()

        advanceUntilIdle()                 // two virtual seconds pass instantly
        assertThat(vm.state.value.saved).isTrue()
    }
}

The classic mistake is asserting before advancing. With StandardTestDispatcher, the coroutine launched in init has not run when the constructor returns, so a test that reads state.value.title straight away sees the default empty title and fails, or worse, passes for the wrong reason.

Step 4: sequences of states with Turbine

When the order of states is the behavior, Turbine collects the flow and lets you await each item:

@Test fun save_emits_saving_then_saved() = runTest {
    repository.saveDelayMs = 1_000         // a suspension between the two updates
    val vm = viewModel()
    advanceUntilIdle()
    vm.onTitleChange("Packing list")

    vm.state.test {
        assertThat(awaitItem().isSaving).isFalse()   // current state
        vm.save()
        assertThat(awaitItem().isSaving).isTrue()
        assertThat(awaitItem().saved).isTrue()
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}

StateFlow is conflated: if two updates happen before the collector runs, it sees only the latest, and equal consecutive values are dropped. A test that expects a state that was immediately replaced waits and times out. That is why the fake has a delay: the suspension between "saving" and "saved" lets the collector see both. Assert on the states that matter, and make sure something suspends between them.

The stateIn trap

A flow exposed with stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList()) runs its upstream only while someone collects it. Reading .value in a test with nobody collecting returns the initial empty list forever. Collect it in backgroundScope, which runTest cancels for you at the end:

backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) {
    vm.notes.collect()
}

Process death, at the ViewModel level

SavedStateHandle has a public constructor that takes a map, so you can simulate the system recreating the ViewModel: write a value through the first instance, build a second one with a handle holding the same values, and assert the state comes back.

val restored = EditorViewModel(repository, SavedStateHandle(mapOf(
    "noteId" to null,
    "draftTitle" to handle.get<String>("draftTitle"),
)))
advanceUntilIdle()
assertThat(restored.state.value.title).isEqualTo("Half-typed")

Checklist

  • The ViewModel depends on interfaces, and each has a reusable fake.
  • A MainDispatcherRule replaces Dispatchers.Main in every ViewModel test.
  • Tests advance (advanceUntilIdle(), runCurrent()) before asserting.
  • Turbine tests have a real suspension between the states they expect.
  • stateIn flows are collected in backgroundScope before reading .value.
  • Saved state is tested by rebuilding the ViewModel from a SavedStateHandle.

Go deeper: Test It Before They Do

item.title: Your fingerprint prompt is a speed bump, not a lock: Android biometrics with a CryptoObject
item.description: Most Android biometric prompts just flip a boolean that a patched APK can flip too, while the data sits unencrypted behind it. Bind a Keystore key to BIOMETRIC_STRONG, pass a CryptoObject, and the prompt releases a key the Keystore guards outside your process. Authenticator classes, key settings and KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException.
item.content:encoded:
A fingerprint prompt feels like security. The user touches the sensor, a little animation plays, the app opens. But look at what most implementations do with the result: onAuthenticationSucceeded() sets a boolean, and the boolean opens the screen. Anyone who can change that boolean, with a debugger on a rooted phone or by patching the APK, opens the screen without a fingerprint. Worse, the data behind the screen was never protected at all; it was sitting in storage the whole time.

A biometric check is only as strong as what it unlocks. This post shows the difference between a prompt that decides a branch in your code and a prompt that releases a cryptographic key, and how to build the second kind with androidx.biometric.

The library

Use the Jetpack Biometric library rather than the platform BiometricPrompt directly. It works back to older Android versions, handles device differences and gives you one API.

dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.biometric:biometric:1.1.0")
}

1.1.0 is the stable release in October 2026. The 1.4.0 alpha line adds an activity-result API, a biometric-compose artifact and KeyAgreement support in CryptoObject; everything below uses the stable BiometricPrompt API, which the alpha keeps.

Strong, weak and the screen lock

BiometricManager.Authenticators defines three types, and the difference between the first two is the whole story:

  • BIOMETRIC_STRONG: a Class 3 biometric under the Android Compatibility Definition. Strong enough to unlock Keystore keys.
  • BIOMETRIC_WEAK: a Class 2 biometric. Can confirm presence, cannot unlock keys.
  • DEVICE_CREDENTIAL: the screen lock (PIN, pattern or password).

The device maker decides which sensor is Class 2 or Class 3, not you. Many face unlock implementations are Class 2 and many fingerprint sensors are Class 3, but do not assume; ask the system.

A few rules from the documentation shape everything:

  • You cannot call setNegativeButtonText() together with DEVICE_CREDENTIAL; when the screen lock is allowed, the system provides its own fallback button.
  • On Android 10 (API level 29) and lower, DEVICE_CREDENTIAL alone and BIOMETRIC_STRONG or DEVICE_CREDENTIAL are not supported combinations. Check for a screen lock with KeyguardManager.isDeviceSecure() instead.
  • Crypto-based authentication is incompatible with Class 2 biometrics, and before Android 11 with the device credential too. Passing a CryptoObject with those authenticators throws IllegalArgumentException.

Check before you prompt

Call canAuthenticate() with exactly the combination you will pass to the prompt:

fun biometricState(context: Context, allowed: Int): BiometricState {
    val manager = BiometricManager.from(context)
    return when (manager.canAuthenticate(allowed)) {
        BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS -> BiometricState.Ready
        BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NONE_ENROLLED -> BiometricState.NeedsEnrollment
        else -> BiometricState.Unavailable    // no hardware, unavailable, update needed
    }
}

When nothing is enrolled, on Android 11 (API level 30) and higher you can send the user to Settings.ACTION_BIOMETRIC_ENROLL, passing the authenticators you accept in Settings.EXTRA_BIOMETRIC_AUTHENTICATORS_ALLOWED. When biometrics are unavailable, fall back to your normal sign-in rather than hiding the feature.

The prompt without crypto, and what it proves

The common version calls showNotes() from onAuthenticationSucceeded(). A successful callback proves only that the system said the user passed, and your code then trusts a callback inside your own process. With a patched APK, or on a device where an attacker controls your process, that callback can be faked, and the notes were readable all along. It is fine for confirming that the person holding an already-unlocked phone is probably the owner before showing something mildly sensitive. It is not a lock.

The prompt with crypto: unlocking a key

The fix is to make the prompt release something the app cannot get any other way. Create a key in the Android Keystore that can only be used after a strong biometric check, and encrypt the sensitive data with it. Now the only way to decrypt is to pass the prompt, because the Keystore enforces the check outside your process, often in secure hardware.

Step 1: an authentication-bound key

private const val KEY_ALIAS = "fieldnotes_vault"

fun createVaultKey() {
    val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
        KEY_ALIAS,
        KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT,
    )
        .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
        .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
        .setKeySize(256)
        .setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)
        // 0 = authenticate for every use; API 30+ form of the setting
        .setUserAuthenticationParameters(0, KeyProperties.AUTH_BIOMETRIC_STRONG)
        .setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)
        .build()
    KeyGenerator.getInstance(KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, "AndroidKeyStore").apply {
        init(spec)
        generateKey()
    }
}
  • setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) makes the key unusable until the user authenticates.
  • setUserAuthenticationParameters(timeout, type), added in API level 30, sets how long a successful authentication keeps the key usable (0 means every operation needs its own prompt) and which kinds count. AUTH_BIOMETRIC_STRONG accepts only Class 3 biometrics; add or KeyProperties.AUTH_DEVICE_CREDENTIAL to accept the screen lock too. Below API 30, the older setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds() does the same job, with -1 meaning per-use.
  • setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) (the default, API 24 and higher) permanently invalidates the key when the user enrolls a new fingerprint or face. Someone who learns the PIN cannot add their own finger and then decrypt.

Step 2: prompt with a CryptoObject

Initialize a Cipher with the key, wrap it in a CryptoObject and pass it to authenticate(). On success, the cipher in the result is authorized for one operation:

val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    .apply { init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, vaultKey()) }

val prompt = BiometricPrompt(activity, ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(activity),
    object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
        override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(
            result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult,
        ) {
            val c = result.cryptoObject?.cipher ?: return
            onDone(EncryptedBlob(iv = c.iv, data = c.doFinal(plaintext)))
        }
    })
prompt.authenticate(
    BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
        .setTitle("Protect your vault")
        .setAllowedAuthenticators(BIOMETRIC_STRONG)
        .setNegativeButtonText("Cancel")
        .build(),
    BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject(cipher),
)

Decryption is the same with Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE and a GCMParameterSpec(128, blob.iv). Store the IV next to the ciphertext; it is not secret, but GCM needs it, and the Keystore generates a fresh random IV for each encryption by default.

Step 3: handle a dead key

When the user adds a new fingerprint or removes the screen lock, the key is gone for good and cipher.init() throws KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException. That is the system doing its job. Catch it, delete the key alias and the ciphertext it protected, and ask the user to sign in again the normal way. Never treat it as a crash:

fun cipherOrNull(mode: Int, iv: ByteArray? = null): Cipher? = try {
    Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding").apply {
        if (iv == null) init(mode, vaultKey())
        else init(mode, vaultKey(), GCMParameterSpec(128, iv))
    }
} catch (e: KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException) {
    KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }.deleteEntry(KEY_ALIAS)
    vaultStore.clear()
    null   // caller falls back to a full sign-in
}

Where it belongs

Good uses: unlocking a stored refresh token so a returning user signs in with a fingerprint; confirming a sensitive action such as deleting the account, where the strongest version signs a server nonce with a biometric-bound private key; and a private vault inside the app with its own authentication-bound key.

Bad uses: a prompt in front of the whole app while the data sits unencrypted behind it, or a prompt treated as a replacement for server-side authentication. After too many failed attempts the system locks biometrics out and reports it through onAuthenticationError(); offer the screen lock or your normal sign-in instead of looping the prompt. And if what you want is "sign in with my fingerprint", passkeys are the better answer, since the credential provider already uses the screen lock and biometrics.

Checklist

  • canAuthenticate() is called with the same authenticators the prompt uses.
  • Anything sensitive is encrypted with a Keystore key that requires BIOMETRIC_STRONG.
  • The prompt passes a CryptoObject, and only the authorized cipher touches the data.
  • Keys are invalidated by new biometric enrollment.
  • KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException leads to a clean re-sign-in, not a crash.
  • A failed or locked-out prompt falls back to the screen lock or normal sign-in.

Go deeper: Sign-In and Security Done Right

item.content:encoded:
Snap it. Know it.

Fieldkey, a new Android app from Hartmann Studios, is now live on Google Play. It identifies plants, rocks, minerals and US coins right on your phone, with no account, no upload and no internet needed.

Three modes in one app

  • Plants: about 2,100 wild and garden species, plus 100 popular houseplants and garden plants, with light, water and pet-safety notes.
  • Rocks: about 130 rocks, minerals, crystals and gemstones, with hardness, streak, crystal system and simple tests you can do at home.

Honest by design

Every result shows how confident the model is and the next-best matches. When it is not sure, it says so and asks for another angle.

Coin values are only ever given as an estimated range, so check a dealer before you sell anything. Plant safety notes are general information, not medical or veterinary advice. Never eat a plant or mushroom because an app said so.

Private and offline

All identification runs on your phone. Your photos never leave the device. There is no account and no analytics, and it works without a connection.

You can save finds to your collection with the photo, date and your own notes, and share a find card with friends.

Free and Pro

The free version gives you 3 identifications a day, plus one more by watching a short video. Pro removes the limit and the ads and adds collection export. It comes as a monthly or yearly subscription (with a free trial) or a one-time lifetime purchase.

Fieldkey is built on open models and open data: the Google AIY plant classifier, photos from iNaturalist and Wikimedia Commons contributors, and descriptions from Wikipedia and Wikidata.

item.title: AuraCast Weather: your forecast as an on-device spoken briefing
item.description: AuraCast Weather turns your forecast into a spoken briefing made on your phone, with live radar, alerts, widgets and offline translation.
item.content:encoded:
Checking the weather usually means reading a screen of icons and numbers while you are trying to get out the door. AuraCast Weather adds another option: a short spoken briefing, written by an AI model on your phone and read aloud in a natural voice, so you can hear the day ahead while you get ready.

What it does

  • Forecasts. Current conditions, a 48-hour hourly forecast and a 5-day forecast, using Open-Meteo and the National Weather Service, with animated weather icons.
  • AI weather podcast. Gemma 4 runs on the device and writes the briefing, then a neural text-to-speech voice reads it aloud. You can pick and preview your favorite voice in Settings.
  • Animated radar. A precipitation radar on a free OpenStreetMap base map, with play, pause and scrub over a 40-minute loop.
  • Translation. On-device translation into 58 languages. The language models download once and then work offline.
  • Alerts. Severe-weather alerts and daily briefing notifications.
  • Everyday touches. Light and dark Material 3 themes, widgets, and support for phones and tablets.

How the briefing is made

The interesting part is where the AI runs. The app fetches the forecast numbers, then hands them to a local model on your phone, which turns them into a natural spoken report. According to the listing, there are no cloud AI calls for the report itself, and the AI report never leaves your device.

That means the briefing does not depend on a remote AI service, and nothing about your morning routine is sent to one. It does still need the internet for the forecast data and radar images.

A hands-free morning

  1. Pick a voice in Settings and preview it.
  2. Turn on the daily briefing notification.
  3. Add a widget to your home screen for a quick glance.
  4. Leave severe-weather alerts on.
  5. If you prefer another language, download its translation model once.

Privacy

The listing spells out the network use:

  • The only network calls are for fetching the forecast and radar imagery.
  • Crash diagnostics use an anonymous install ID.
  • Ads follow Google's Advertising ID policies, with a consent prompt where required.
  • No account is required.

Good to know

  • AuraCast Weather is free to download and contains ads.
  • No account is needed.
  • The app is open source; the listing links to its code repository.
  • The forecast sources include the National Weather Service, so some data is specific to the United States.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Weather category.

Is it for you?

  • You would rather hear the forecast than read it.
  • You want the AI part to run on your own phone, not in the cloud.
  • You check the radar before heading out.
  • You want severe-weather alerts and a home screen widget.
  • You like apps that publish their source code.

item.title: How Shape & Shade maps a face on your phone
item.description: A look under the hood: 478 face points from an on-device model, four measurements, plain-math shape matching, and why the app shows the lines instead of a verdict.
item.content:encoded:
Shape & Shade answers one question, "what's my face shape?", without sending your face anywhere. Here's how it does that on the phone.

Step 1: find the face points

The app runs Google's MediaPipe Face Landmarker on the device (the float16 model, about 3.8 MB, bundled in the app). It returns 478 three-dimensional points: the outline of the face, the brows, eyes, irises, nose, lips and jaw. This is the only "AI" in the face-shape scan. Everything after it is ordinary arithmetic.

Step 2: measure

From those points the app takes four measurements:

  • Forehead width, across the top of the face
  • Cheekbone width, the widest line across the cheekbones
  • Jaw width, across the angles of the jaw
  • Face length, from the hairline area to the chin

It also looks at how sharp or soft the jawline is and how narrow the chin is. Dividing these gives ratios that don't depend on how far you held the phone: length to width, forehead to jaw, jaw to cheekbones.

Step 3: match, and say how sure

Each of the six shapes (oval, round, square, heart, diamond, oblong) has a reference set of ratios. The app measures how close your ratios are to each one. The closest is your shape. If the runner-up is nearly as close, the result says so ("between heart and oval") instead of pretending to be sure. That's why the result is called an estimate from your measurements.

Step 4: show the work

The result screen draws the measurement lines on your photo and lists the reasons in plain words, for example "Your forehead is wider than your jaw" or "Your jawline is softly curved". You can check it yourself.

What stays on the phone

The model, the photo, the points and the result. There's no account and nothing is uploaded. Pro's Color Season scan works the same way: a second on-device model (MediaPipe's selfie segmenter) separates skin, hair and clothes, and the colors are compared in CIELAB space with a white sheet of paper for white balance. Color season is for fun and style ideas.

What it doesn't do

No beauty scores, and no guessing at age, ethnicity or gender. The guides suggest; they don't judge.

item.description: CruiseLoom keeps your cruise itinerary, port weather and route map on your phone, with nearby chat for your group over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct.
item.content:encoded:
A cruise is a strange place to rely on your phone. Internet at sea can be slow, expensive or missing, your plans change port by port, and your group scatters across a ship the size of a small town. CruiseLoom is a cruise companion built around that reality: your itinerary works offline, weather is cached for weak connections, and your party can chat nearby without the internet.

What it does

  • Voyage planning. Set your ship and sailing dates, see sea days, port days and upcoming plans at a glance, and add dinners, shows, excursions and local reminders.
  • Port prep. Search and organize real port stops, check current conditions and a seven-day forecast, and cache recent weather for patchy connections.
  • Route map. View your itinerary on a route map built on OpenStreetMap.
  • Deck plans. Download optional ship-deck schematics for supported ships.
  • Nearby group chat. Add shipmates with a QR code generated on your phone, then chat over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct using broadcast or private messages.
  • Guest chat. Host temporary guest Wi-Fi chat for companions who do not have the app.

Before you sail

  2. Add your port stops and check each one's forecast.
  3. Put dinners, shows and excursions on the right days, with reminders.
  4. Download the deck schematics if your ship is supported.

Keeping the group together

The chat feature does not depend on the ship's internet. Shipmates scan a locally generated QR code to join, and messages travel directly between nearby phones over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct. You can send a message to everyone or privately to one person. For a companion without the app, you can host a temporary guest Wi-Fi chat instead.

Where your data lives

The listing is clear about this: CruiseLoom stores cruise plans and chat history locally on your device, and Android cloud backup is disabled. Online services are used only for features such as weather, maps, optional deck downloads, diagnostics and advertising, as explained in the app's privacy policy. Because backup is off, plans live only on that phone.

item.title: CruiseWatch: get alerted when your booked cruise fare drops
item.description: CruiseWatch tracks the public fare on a cruise you already booked and alerts you when it drops, with the claim steps and deadline for your line.
item.content:encoded:
Booking a cruise is usually not the end of the price story. Fares keep moving after you pay your deposit, and many cruise lines will refund the difference or give onboard credit if the price drops before your final payment date. The catch: you have to notice the drop and ask before the window closes. CruiseWatch does the noticing.

What it does

  • Watches your booked cruise. Add your ship, sail date and cabin category, and CruiseWatch checks the public fare.
  • Covers five lines. Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Carnival, Princess and Norwegian.
  • Instant push alerts. When a lower fare appears, you get the new price and how much you are owed.
  • Exact next steps. Each alert shows the cruise line's phone number, a ready-to-read script, and your claim deadline, based on that line's price-drop or "Best Price Guarantee" policy.
  • On-device AI refund assistant. Ask questions about a specific alert and get step-by-step help claiming a refund or onboard credit.
  • Wear OS companion. Installed automatically with the phone app, it shows price-drop alerts and your claim history on your watch.
  • Home screen widget. Check status at a glance.

How a claim works

The flow is short:

  1. Add each cruise you have already booked: ship, sail date and cabin category.
  2. Let CruiseWatch watch the public pricing.
  3. When an alert arrives, read the new price and the amount you are owed.
  4. Call the number shown in the alert, using the script provided.
  5. Do it before the claim deadline in the alert.

The script and deadline are the useful part. Policies differ by line, and the app pulls the steps from each line's own price-drop policy instead of leaving you to search for the terms.

Privacy

The AI refund assistant runs entirely on your device and works fully offline, and the listing states that your booking details never leave your phone when you use it.

Good to know

  • CruiseWatch is free to use with ads, and there is an optional ad-free monthly subscription.
  • It only works with cruises already booked on Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Carnival, Princess or Norwegian.
  • CruiseWatch is an independent tool and is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by any cruise line.
  • Pricing and policy information is provided for reference only. Always confirm current terms directly with your cruise line before requesting a refund; a refund or credit is never guaranteed by the app.
  • Most lines only honor a drop before your final payment date, so add your cruise as soon as you book.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Travel and Local category.

Is it for you?

  • You have a cruise booked with one of the five supported lines.
  • Your final payment date has not passed yet.
  • You would rather get a push alert than check fares by hand every week.
  • You want the phone number, script and deadline ready when a drop happens.
  • You wear a Wear OS watch and like alerts on your wrist.

item.title: Real HTTPS for your homelab without opening a single port
item.description: Self-signed warnings, a private CA nobody can install, or port forwarding? None of them. Here is the fix from Containers Without the Chaos - Caddy, a DNS-01 wildcard certificate and split DNS, so every internal app gets a real padlock and nothing is exposed.
item.content:encoded:
You want https://notes.home.example.com to open with a padlock and no warning on every device in the house, including the phones of guests you will never install a certificate on. And you want it without opening a single port to the internet. Containers Without the Chaos covers this in two chapters: a reverse proxy done right, then real HTTPS for internal names.

The trap: three half-solutions

There are three common ways people try this, and each one fails in its own way:

  • Self-signed certificates. Every browser warns, every family member learns to click "continue anyway", and that habit is the real security problem.
  • A private certificate authority. It works, but every device needs the CA installed, and many phones, TVs and apps make that hard.
  • Port forwarding 80 and 443 so the normal HTTP challenge works. Now your internal apps are reachable from the internet, which is the opposite of the goal.

The fix: the DNS-01 challenge

To issue a certificate, a public certificate authority such as Let's Encrypt has to check that you control the name. With the DNS challenge, the CA does an authoritative DNS lookup for a special TXT record, and if it sees the expected value, it issues the certificate. No open ports, and the server asking for the certificate never has to be reachable from outside.

You need two things:

  1. A real domain you own, with its DNS hosted at a provider that has an API and a Caddy DNS module (Cloudflare and many others have one; the module list is on caddyserver.com/download).
  2. An API token that lets Caddy create and delete TXT records in that zone.

Names under .local, .internal and .home.arpa cannot get publicly trusted certificates. Use a subdomain of a real domain you own, such as home.example.com.

One wildcard for everything

Instead of one certificate per app, ask for one wildcard: *.home.example.com. It covers notes.home.example.com, photos.home.example.com and anything you add later. Wildcards require the DNS challenge, and a certificate may have only one wildcard, as the left-most label.

There is a privacy bonus. Certificates are published in public Certificate Transparency logs, so per-app certificates would list every internal app name for anyone to read. A wildcard reveals only *.home.example.com.

Build Caddy with a DNS module

The standard Caddy image does not include DNS provider modules, so build your own with the official builder image and xcaddy. Create /srv/stacks/proxy/Dockerfile (Cloudflare shown; use your provider's module):

FROM caddy:2.11-builder AS builder
RUN xcaddy build \
    --with github.com/caddy-dns/cloudflare

FROM caddy:2.11
COPY --from=builder /usr/bin/caddy /usr/bin/caddy

Point the proxy stack at it instead of the plain image. Ports, volumes and networks stay as in the proxy chapter (80, 443 and 443/udp; the ./conf folder mounted at /etc/caddy; ./data for certificates; the external proxy network):

services:
  caddy:
    build: .
    image: local/caddy-dns:2.11
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: ./caddy.env

Build, start and confirm the module is in:

docker compose build --pull
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec caddy caddy list-modules | grep dns

The API token

Create a token at your DNS provider that can edit DNS records in this one zone and nothing else. Put it in caddy.env, readable only by you, and keep the file out of Git:

CF_API_TOKEN=paste-the-token-here
chmod 600 /srv/stacks/proxy/caddy.env

That token can change DNS for your whole domain. Scope it to the single zone and to DNS edit only. If it leaks, revoke it at the provider and create a new one.

The wildcard Caddyfile

Put every internal site inside one wildcard site block and pick the app with a host matcher. This is the pattern from Caddy's "Common Caddyfile Patterns" page:

*.home.example.com {
    tls {
        dns cloudflare {env.CF_API_TOKEN}
    }

    @notes host notes.home.example.com
    handle @notes {
        reverse_proxy notes:8080
    }

    @photos host photos.home.example.com
    handle @photos {
        reverse_proxy photos:2283
    }

    handle {
        abort
    }
}

The last handle block catches any name you have not defined and closes the connection, so a typo does not land on some other app. Since Caddy 2.10, separate site blocks per app also use an automated wildcard certificate; the single block just keeps the tls settings in one place.

Reload without downtime and watch for the certificate:

docker compose exec -w /etc/caddy caddy caddy reload
docker compose logs caddy | grep -i -E "certificate|obtain"

While testing, add acme_ca https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory inside the tls block. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers, but staging has much looser rate limits. Remove the line once it works. And never delete ./data to "start fresh": it holds every certificate Caddy has obtained, and certificate authorities enforce rate limits.

Split DNS: names that only exist at home

The certificate proves the names are yours. Now your network has to answer them. Your public DNS zone does not need any record for *.home.example.com at all; only your local resolver answers it, pointing every name at the Docker VM.

On OPNsense with Unbound, add one host override: host *, domain home.example.com, address 192.168.20.10. If your resolver does not support wildcard overrides, add one override per app. In plain Unbound configuration it looks like this:

server:
  local-zone: "home.example.com." redirect
  local-data: "home.example.com. 300 IN A 192.168.20.10"

Check from a laptop on the LAN:

dig +short notes.home.example.com
# 192.168.20.10
curl -I https://notes.home.example.com

If a name resolves on the Docker VM but not on a laptop, suspect DNS rebinding protection. Some resolvers and routers refuse answers that point a public domain at a private address. Check the resolver's rebind settings and allow your internal domain.

Away from home

Nothing here is reachable from the internet, by design. To use these names away from home, connect to your network over WireGuard or Tailscale and make sure the VPN hands out your local resolver. The same names and the same certificate then work everywhere.

Checklist

  • A subdomain of a real domain you own, never .local, .internal or .home.arpa
  • Caddy built with your DNS provider's module, and caddy list-modules | grep dns shows it
  • An API token scoped to one zone and DNS edit only, in caddy.env with chmod 600, kept out of Git
  • One *.home.example.com block with a host matcher per app and a final handle { abort }
  • Staging CA while testing, removed once the certificate arrives; ./data kept and backed up
  • A local DNS override pointing *.home.example.com at the Docker VM, nothing in the public zone
  • Rebind protection allows your internal domain; dig and curl -I pass from a laptop
  • Remote access through WireGuard or Tailscale, handing out your local resolver
  • No ports 80 or 443 forwarded from the internet

item.title: Looki L1 mount v9: snug holder + slide-in collar clips (free STL)
item.description: Version 9 of the free 3D-printed Looki L1 wearable camera mount. A snug holder sized for the bare camera and two collar clips that slide in on dovetail rails and click locked. STL downloads, the exact ABS print settings and the real print timelapse.
item.content:encoded:
The free Looki L1 mount is on version 9, and this is the one to print now. It has a new holder that fits the bare camera snugly and two new collar clips (thick and thin) that slide into the back of the holder on full-width dovetail rails and click locked with a small button.

What changed from the last version

  • Holder: the older pocket was sized for the Looki wearing its silicone case, so the bare camera had about 2.4 mm of play on each side. The v9 pocket is the bare Looki plus 0.25 mm per side, with four small snap bumps (0.6 mm over the edge, just above the widest rim) that hold it in. The lens, button and back windows are unchanged.
  • Clips: the old clips only had a dovetail on one side and the tongue stopped half way, so they could pop out. The v9 clips slide in sideways, from the right. That way both rails, top and bottom, are part of the clip's side profile, so they print cleanly and run the clip's full width.
  • Lock: a 1.3 mm flex beam under the rails carries a small button that clicks into a 4.2 mm hole in the holder. The weight hangs on the rails, not on the button.
  • The safety lanyard frame is not part of this release. It's coming in a later update.

Printed and assembled

These photos are the real v9 parts, printed in black ABS.

Downloads

  • looki_v9_holder.stl (964 KB): the holder the Looki snaps into
  • looki_v9_clip_thick.stl (98 KB): the thick collar clip, 32 mm wide
  • looki_v9_clip_thin.stl (101 KB): the thin collar clip, 26 mm wide
  • looki_v9_abs_profile.ini: the PrusaSlicer profile the parts in the photos were printed with
  • Everything as one zip

Also on Printables, where the older v4 files are still available too. License: CC BY 4.0, Charles Hartmann / Homelab the Right Way.

How the clip goes on and comes off

  1. Slide the clip into the channel on the back of the holder from the right side. The rails guide it, and the closed left end is the stop.
  2. Push until the button clicks into the hole in the holder.
  3. To take it off, press the thumb tab toward the shirt and slide the clip out to the right. With the Looki out, you can also push the button from the inside.

Pick the thick or the thin clip, whichever fits your collar better.

Print settings

What the parts in the photos were printed with:

  • Material: ABS, 240 C nozzle and 100 C bed.
  • Layers: 0.2 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 4 perimeters, 40% gyroid infill. No supports.
  • Raft: an easy-peel raft, 3 raft layers with a 0.3 mm contact gap and no raft expansion. It keeps the ABS flat and comes off clean.
  • Orientation: print as exported. The clips print on their side, so the layer lines run around the bend and the arm flexes instead of snapping.
  • Time: the plate in the timelapse (the holder, both clips and the lanyard frame that isn't released yet) took 8 h 22 min.

The timelapse at the top of this page is the real v9 plate printing, straight off the OctoPrint camera.

Fit notes

The Looki outline is based on the camera's official 50.53 x 48.02 mm size. If the holder is too tight or too loose on yours, or a clip is too stiff or too loose on the rails, leave a comment on the Printables page saying which part.

The original v4 cradle and clip, with the screw-on design, are still written up in the first Looki mount post.

Not affiliated with Looki. The Looki L1 is a product of looki.ai; this is an independent, free accessory. The model was designed with AI help and printed and tested on a real printer.
